title: Sortilin deficiency improves the metabolic phenotype and reduces hepatic steatosis of mice subjected to diet-induced obesity.
text_summary: 本研究旨在探究Sortilin缺陷对饮食诱导肥胖（DIO）小鼠代谢表型和肝脂肪变性影响。通过高脂饮食喂养C57BL/6（WT）和Sortilin-/-小鼠10周，发现Sortilin-/-小鼠体重和内脏脂肪积累均低于WT小鼠，且胰岛素耐量试验中葡萄糖摄取增强，肝pAkt表达增加。Sortilin缺陷导致肝脂肪变性减轻，脂生成、鞘氨醇合成和炎症细胞因子产生相关基因表达降低，CerS5/6活性降低。Sortilin-/-小鼠在稳态和DIO状态下均表现出降低的肝aSMase活性。同样，Sortilin-/-脂肪组织炎症细胞因子表达降低，CerS5/6表达和活性降低，且胰岛素信号通路增强，aSMase活性降低。结论：Sortilin缺陷通过降低aSMase活性，在DIO状态下诱导肝脏和脂肪组织有益的代谢表型。

Sortilin deﬁciency improves the metabolic phenotype and
reduces hepatic steatosis of mice subjected to diet-induced obesity
Liane Rabinowich1,, Sigal Fishman1,, Einav Hubel1, Tamar Thurm2, Woo-Jae Park3,4,
Yael Pewzner-Jung3, Ashish Saroha3, Noam Erez1, Zamir Halpern1,
Anthony H. Futerman3, Isabel Zvibel1,⇑
1The Research Center for Digestive Tract and Liver Diseases, Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center and the Sackler Faculty of Medicine,
Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel; 2Internal Medicine D, Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center, Tel Aviv, Israel; 3Department of Biological
Chemistry, Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot, Israel; 4Department of Biochemistry, School of Medicine, Gachon University,
Incheon 406-799, Republic of Korea
Background & Aims: Sortilin trafﬁcs newly synthesized mole-
cules from the trans-Golgi apparatus along secretory pathways
to endosomes, lysosomes or to the cell surface. Sortilin trafﬁcking
of acid sphingomyelinase (aSMase) may regulate ceramide levels,
a major modulator of insulin signalling. We therefore tested
whether sortilin deﬁciency reduces hepatic and adipose tissue
aSMase activity, improving insulin sensitivity in diet-induced
obesity (DIO).
Methods: DIO in C57BL/6 (WT) and sortilin/ mice was induced
by high-fat diet feeding for 10 weeks.
Results: Sortilin/ mice gained less body weight and less vis-
ceral fat, despite similar food intake compared to WT type mice
and had enhanced glucose uptake in insulin tolerance tests,
which was further corroborated by enhanced hepatic pAkt
expression. Sortilin deﬁciency led to attenuated hepatic steatosis,
reduced expression of genes involved in lipogenesis, ceramide
synthesis and inﬂammatory cytokine production and reduced
activity of ceramide synthase 5/6 (CerS5/6). Sortilin/ mice
had reduced hepatic aSMase activity under both steady-state
and DIO. Likewise, sortilin/ hepatocytes displayed hypersensi-
tivity to insulin, due to enhanced insulin receptor downstream
signalling. In adipose tissue, sortilin/ mice exhibited lower
expression of inﬂammatory cytokines and lower expression and
activity of CerS5/6. As in liver, adipose tissue displayed increased
insulin signalling, accompanied by attenuated aSMase activity.
Conclusions: Sortilin deﬁciency induces a beneﬁcial metabolic
phenotype in liver and adipose tissue upon DIO, mediated in part
by reduced aSMase activity.

Introduction
Obesity has become a world-wide epidemic in western countries,
leading to insulin resistance, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and
non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). NAFLD is commonly
associated with insulin resistance and characterized by hepatic
accumulation of triglycerides (TGs) [1].
Sortilin is a member of the vacuolar protein sorting 10 protein
(VPS10P)-domain receptor family. Sortilin functions both as a
co-receptor and as a trafﬁcking molecule that binds and directs
newly synthesized molecules from the trans-Golgi network
(TGN) to regulated secretion pathways, including endosomes,
lysosomes or to the cell surface [2]. Recent studies have
implicated sortilin in several metabolic processes in the liver
and adipose tissue [2–4]. Human genome wide association
studies (GWAS) indicate a strong association of a speciﬁc SNP
in the SORT1 gene with decreased serum levels of low-density
lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and myocardial infarction [3].
Following this discovery, sortilin was shown to control plasma
LDL by two possible mechanisms. In the ﬁrst, sortilin modulates
LDL secretion by binding to ApoB in the Golgi and directing it
towards the cell surface and secretion, or towards a degradation
pathway [3–4]. In the second, sortilin regulates LDL catabolism
by uptake of circulating serum LDL and transferring it to lyso-
somes for degradation [3–6]. Recently, sortilin was shown to
inﬂuence sphingolipid metabolism by trafﬁcking acid sphingo-
myelinase (aSMase) to the lysosome or cell surface, as well as
by participating in the trafﬁcking of sphingolipid activation
proteins (SAPs) [7–9].
ASMase and neutral-sphingomyelinase 2 (nSMase) regulate
the turnover of sphingomyelin (SM), to produce ceramide in

the lysosome or at the cell surface [10–11]. Ceramide contributes
to insulin resistance and lipotoxicity by suppressing IRS-1
phosphorylation, thereby reducing insulin signalling [12–14]. In
addition to its role in the regulation of ceramide levels, aSMase
modulates the partitioning of diet-derived palmitate into two
competitive and inversely correlated lipid pools, sphingolipids
(SLs) and TGs [15]. Interestingly, aSMase//LDLR/ mice show
attenuated diet-induced hepatic TG accumulation and improved
insulin sensitivity compared to LDLR/ mice [15].
We hypothesized that sortilin deﬁciency, which results in
reduced activity of lysosomal and/or cell surface hepatic and adi-
pose tissue aSMase, and thus reduced ceramide levels, may lead
to improved insulin sensitivity and reduced hepatic TG accumu-
lation in diet-induced obesity (DIO). Thus, we investigated the
connection between sortilin deﬁciency, aSMase activity, insulin
sensitivity and hepatic steatosis in DIO.
Materials and methods
Animals and diets
Wild type (WT) male C57BL/6 mice (Harlan) and sortilin/ male mice, obtained
by introduction of the neo gene into exon 14 and the following intron of the sor-
tilin gene [16] (a generous gift of Prof. A. Nykjaer, Aarhus University, Denmark)
were fed ad libitum with regular rat chow (RC) (64% carbohydrate, 30% protein,
and 6% fat) or a rodent high fat diet (HFD) from Research Diets (New Brunswick,
NJ) with 60% kcal from fat (#D12492, 26% protein, 26% carbohydrate and 36% fat).
Thirty min before sacriﬁce, mice were injected i.p. with 0.75 U/kg body weight
insulin. Serum was taken for the measurement of metabolic and adipokine anal-
ysis. Liver and epididymal adipose tissue were frozen in liquid nitrogen and kept
at 80 C for biochemical and molecular analysis. Liver and adipose tissue were
ﬁxed in formaldehyde for histochemical and morphological assays. The studies
were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Tel Aviv Sourasky Med-
ical Center.
Insulin tolerance test (ITT)
Mice were fasted for 4 h, and basal glucose was measured using the AccuCheck
sensor blood glucometer. Insulin (0.75 U/kg body weight) was administered by
i.p. injection, followed by serum glucose measurements 30, 60, and 120 min
later.
Assays and analytical procedures
Hepatic triglycerides (TGs) and hepatic cholesterol and serum ALT, AST, TGs and
cholesterol were measured using a Hitachi 747 Automatic Analyzer.
Murine hepatocyte isolation and culture
Livers of male C57BL/6 mice (WT) and male sortilin/ mice were perfused with
0.5 mM EDTA, then with a solution containing 25 mg/ml collagenase type II
(Worthington). Hepatocytes were plated on collagen I-coated plates in DMEM,
supplemented with 10% FCS. After 4 h, the medium was changed to hormonally
deﬁned medium (HDM) without insulin for 16 h. The composition of the HDM
was as described by Block et al., [17] with modiﬁcations: DMEM supplemented
with 100 lg/ml penicillin and streptomycin, 2 mg/ml bovine serum albumin,
610 lg/ml nicotinamide, 740 ng/ml ZnSO4:7H2O, 20 ng/ml CuSO4:5H2O, 5 mM
glutamine,
5 lg/ml
iron-saturated
transferrin,
5 ng/ml
selenious
acid
and
107 M dexamethasone. The next day, hepatocytes were treated with 100 nM
insulin for 7 and 20 min and protein was extracted.
Western blots
Protein from liver or adipose tissue was extracted by homogenization in ice-cold
RIPA buffer (PBS, 1% NP40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, 1 mM PMSF,
aprotinin 5 lg/ml, leupeptin 10 lg/ml, pepstatin A 1 lg/ml and phosphatase
inhibitor cocktail). Homogenates were centrifuged for 25 min at 13,000 g, super-
natants were collected and protein concentration was determined. Total protein
from adipose tissue explants was extracted by incubation for 30 min on ice in
lysis buffer (250 mmol/L sucrose, 5 mmol/L MgCl2, 10 mmol/L Tris pH 8.0, 0.5%
Triton X-100, protease and phosphatase inhibitors). Proteins were separated by
SDS-PAGE, blotted onto Hybond C extra and blocked overnight in 5% milk. Blots
were incubated with antibodies to pAkt (dilution 1:1000, Cell Signaling Technol-
ogy, Danvers, MA) and Akt1/2 (dilution 1:1000), fatty acid synthase (FAS) (dilu-
tion 1:1000) or b-actin (dilution 1:5000) (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz,
CA), then incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibod-
ies and subjected to chemiluminescent detection.
aSMase activity assays
aSMase activity from liver and adipose tissue extracts was assessed as described
[18–19]. Brieﬂy, liver or adipose tissue was homogenated in sodium acetate
buffer (50 mM sodium acetate, pH 4.5) with protease inhibitor (Sigma). Protein
concentration was measured using a BCA protein assay kit (Pierce Chemical
Co.), 50 lg of protein was used for the assay. The assay was started by addition
of 1 nmol C6–NBD-SM (Avanti Polar Lipids) into 0.5 ml of sodium acetate buffer
(including 50 lg of protein), incubated at 37 C for 15 min and stopped by the
addition of 1.5 ml of chloroform/methanol (1:2; v/v). Lipids were separated by
thin layer chromatography (TLC) using chloroform/methanol: 9.8 mM CaCl2
(60:35:8; v/v/v). TLCs were scanned by a Typhon scanner (GE Life Sciences) and
quantiﬁed using ImageQuant software (GE Life Sciences).
CerS activity assay
Liver and adipose tissues were homogenized in 20 mM Hepes (pH 7.2), 25 mM
KCl, 250 mM sucrose, and 2 mM MgCl2 containing a protease inhibitor mixture
(Sigma). Protein was determined using the BCA reagent (Pierce). Homogenates
(12 lg protein) were incubated with 15 lM N-(7-nitro-2-1,3-benzoxadiazole-4-
yl) (2S, 3R)-2-aminooctadecane-1,3-diol (NBD-sphinganine [Avanti Polar Lipids]),
20 lM defatted BSA (Sigma), and 50 lM C16-CoA (Avanti Polar Lipids) for 15 min
at 37 C. Lipids were extracted and separated by TLC using chloroform/methanol/
water and 2 M NH4OH (40:10:0.75:0.25; vol/vol/vol) as the developing solvent.
NBD-labelled lipids were visualized using the Typhoon 9410 variable mode
imager and quantiﬁed by ImageQuant TL software (GE Healthcare).
Quantitative real time RT-PCR
Total RNA was extracted from livers using the EZ-RNA kit (Biological Industries,
Bet Haemek, Israel) and from adipose tissue using the RNeasy lipid tissue kit
(Qiagen) and 2.5 lg total RNA was reverse-transcribed using the reverse trans-
criptase enzyme MMLV (Promega, Madison, WI). Real time RT-PCR (qRT-PCR)

fat) for 10 weeks. The model was established using C57BL/6 male
mice (WT) or sortilin/ male mice [16]. After 10 weeks of HFD
feeding, sortilin/ mice had gained signiﬁcantly less body weight
and less perinephric and epididymal fat tissue mass, despite sim-
ilar food intake, compared to WT mice on the same diet (Table 1).
Sortilin/ mice displayed a signiﬁcantly better insulin toler-
ance test (ITT) compared to wild type (WT) control mice after
HFD feeding, indicating reduced development of insulin resis-
tance under diet-induced obesity (DIO) (Fig. 1A), along with
increased pAkt expression (Fig. 1B). Moreover, the expression
levels of glucose 6-phosphatase (G6Pase), which is involved in
gluconeogenesis and is inhibited by downstream insulin receptor
signalling, was still strongly reduced in sortilin/ mice, further
indicating that these mice retained a better insulin response
compared to WT mice under DIO (Fig. 1C).
In addition, we assessed the in vitro response of hepatocytes
isolated from WT and sortilin/ mice to insulin. Cultured
primary hepatocytes were stimulated with 100 nM insulin for 7
or 20 min, then pAkt expression was assessed; hepatocytes from
sortilin/ mice had a higher and more sustained response to
insulin compared to WT hepatocytes (Fig. 1D).
Sortilin/ mice have reduced hepatic steatosis in the DIO model
Examination of liver sections revealed that after 10 weeks of HFD
WT mice developed steatosis, while livers of sortilin/ mice dis-
played almost no steatosis (Fig. 2A), which was also corroborated
by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 2A). In addition, sortilin/ mice had a
signiﬁcantly reduced hepatic content of triglycerides (TGs) and
slightly reduced hepatic cholesterol, although this did not reach
a statically signiﬁcant level (Table 1). We next examined the
expression of genes involved in TG synthesis (Fig. 2B). In line with
the reduced hepatic TG content (Table 1), sortilin/ mice dis-
played reduced mRNA levels of lipogenesis genes FAS and SCD1
(Fig. 2B), as well as reduced protein levels of FAS (Fig. 2C). The
reduced TG levels could also be due to increased b-oxidation,
however, this process was not signiﬁcantly altered in the livers
of sortilin/ mice fed with HFD, as demonstrated by levels of
carnitine palmitoyltransferase (CPT1) (Fig. 2B).
We next examined expression of genes involved in de novo
ceramide synthesis. Sortilin/ mice had reduced mRNA expres-
sion of the rate-limiting enzyme, regulating de novo ceramide
synthesis, namely serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT1) (Fig. 3A).
In addition, hepatic mRNA expression of ceramide synthases 5
and 6 (CerS5/6) were also signiﬁcantly lower in sortilin/ mice
(Fig. 3A), as was CerS5/6 activity after DIO (Fig. 3B). CerS5/6 activ-
ity was similar in WT and sortilin/ mice under rat chow (RC)
(Fig. 3B). In addition, when we assessed the mRNA expression
of hepatic inﬂammatory, insulin-inhibiting cytokines, we found
a signiﬁcant reduction in the inﬂammatory cytokines TNFa, IL-6,
and IL-1b in the livers of sortilin/ mice (Fig. 3C), including the
inﬂammatory cytokine progranulin (PRGN). Finally, sortilin/
mice had signiﬁcantly reduced hepatic aSMase activity both
under steady-state condition and after 10 weeks of HFD (Fig. 3D).
Adipose tissue of sortilin/ mice has better insulin sensitivity,
reduced aSMase activity and improved metabolic and inﬂammatory
phenotype after DIO compared to WT mice
Adipose tissue of sortilin/ mice displayed dramatically reduced
inﬂammatory cell inﬁltration after DIO, as well as signiﬁcantly
reduced adipocyte area (Fig. 4A and B). Similarly to the hepatic
phenotype,
adipose
tissue

sortilin/
mice
showed
increased Akt phosphorylation when compared to pAkt in WT
mice (Fig. 4C). In addition, and again similar to the liver results,
mRNA of CerS6 was found to be signiﬁcantly reduced in the adi-
pose tissue of sortilin/ mice after DIO (Fig. 4D), as was CerS5/6
activity (Fig. 4E). However, in contrast to the liver, adipose tissue
of sortilin/ mice had increased mRNA expression of lipogenesis
enzymes, including FAS and SCD1 (Fig. 4F), but also increased
expression
of

transcription

(Fig. 4F), suggesting increased fat burning. With regard to inﬂam-
matory cytokine expression, TNFa, IL-6, and PRGN [18] were
reduced, while adiponectin was signiﬁcantly increased (Fig. 4G).
Interestingly, sortilin is known to internalize serum PRGN [20],
and as expected, sortilin/ mice had signiﬁcantly higher serum
PRGN compared to WT controls after DIO (Table 1). Finally,
sortilin/ adipose tissue had signiﬁcantly lower aSMase activity
compared to WT control tissue (Fig. 4H).

Discussion
Our study showed a beneﬁcial effect of sortilin deﬁciency on
insulin sensitivity in a murine model of diet-induced obesity
(DIO). We have linked sortilin, known to trafﬁc aSMase to the cell
surface, with aSMase activity and the resulting metabolic changes
in DIO. Sortilin deﬁciency enhanced hepatic and adipose tissue
insulin signalling in vivo after DIO and was accompanied by
reduced aSMase activity. Sortilin deﬁciency led to dramatically
attenuated hepatic steatosis and inﬂammation, better insulin
sensitivity and reduced inﬂammation in the adipose tissue of
sortilin/ mice after DIO, compared to their WT counterparts
on the same diet. We attribute at least part of the beneﬁcial effect
of sortilin deﬁciency to the reduced activity of aSMase, an
enzyme responsible for the turnover of sphingomyelin and
production of ceramide [21].

role both as a co-receptor when present on the cell surface and

In its role as a trafﬁcking molecule, sortilin directs several newly
synthesized molecules to the endosomal and lysosomal compart-
ments, as well as to the cell surface [2]. Several of the molecules
whose trafﬁcking is regulated by sortilin are proteins and
enzymes involved in the regulation of lipid and glucose metabo-
lism. Human genome wide association studies (GWAS) have iden-
tiﬁed an association between a SNP leading to increased hepatic
levels of sortilin and reduced levels of serum low-density lipopro-
tein (LDL) [3]. In contrast to the human studies, double knockout
mice for sortilin and LDL receptor display reduced hepatic secre-
tion of LDL, reduced serum LDL and attenuated atherosclerotic
lesion formation [4]. Regulation of LDL levels is the most thor-
oughly investigated effect of sortilin on lipid metabolism.
Since several of the molecules trafﬁcked by sortilin, such as
aSMase and sphingolipid activator proteins (SAPs), are involved
in the regulation of cellular ceramide levels, we investigated this
aspect of the sortilin effect on diet-induced insulin resistance
[7–9].
Our studies demonstrate reduced aSMase activity in both liver
and adipose tissue of sortilin/ mice under DIO. So far, sortilin
has only been shown to trafﬁc aSMase to the lysosomes or to
the cell surface [7–9], but we are the ﬁrst to detect an association
between the absence of sortilin, reduced aSMase activity, and
retained insulin sensitivity. Indeed, aSMase deﬁciency has been
linked to enhanced insulin sensitivity, due perhaps to reduced
ceramide levels [21].
In addition to aSMase-derived ceramide, ceramide levels are
also regulated by de novo synthesis and by the salvage pathway
[22–25]. Diet-derived palmitate can be used to synthesize either
sphingolipids or triglycerides, the rate-limiting enzyme control-
ling this step being SPT1 [22–25]. SPT1 directs palmitate towards
sphingolipids and ceramide synthesis. Notably, sortilin/ mice
under DIO had reduced mRNA expression of SPT1 as well as
reduced hepatic and adipose tissue expression and activity of
ceramide synthase 6 (CerS6) from the de novo pathway.
Different CerS generate speciﬁc ceramides, with different acyl
chains, which may exert different functions [26–27]. Importantly,
CerS6 which is responsible for generation of C16-ceramides has
been linked to hepatic insulin resistance [28]. This is particularly
relevant in view of the debate about whether hepatic ceramide is
a direct cause of insulin resistance [29–30]. For instance, a study
using double knockout mice for aSMase and LDL receptor showed
increased hepatic accumulation of sphingolipids and ceramide,
with improved insulin sensitivity, suggesting that increased cer-
amide levels in the liver may not always induce insulin resistance
[15]. It should be noted that this model is different to our model,
due to reduced hepatic LDL uptake. In addition, ceramides with
different acyl chains may differentially affect insulin sensitivity.
Moreover, sortilin/ mice exhibited attenuated hepatic TG
synthesis, accompanied by reduced hepatic TG accumulation
and lack of hepatic steatosis, which may be attributed to the
reduced development of insulin resistance. Similarly to the liver,
adipose tissue of sortilin/ mice also displayed better insulin
response, reduced aSMase activity and reduced levels of CerS6.
Although expression of lipogenesis enzymes and TG uptake regu-
lating lipoprotein lipase (LPL) were increased in adipose tissue of
sortilin/ mice, there was no increase in their fat mass, which
may be due to increased b-oxidation of lipids, as suggested by
increased PPARa levels.
In conclusion, we show a novel role for sortilin in the regula-
tion of insulin sensitivity, via regulation of aSMase activity.
